divergence: jsntrs answered [1,2,3,4,5] before jsntrs-uql, because `..` was an ordinary infix operator. docs.jsonata.org/numeric-operators, '.. (Range)': 'The sequence generator can only be used within an array constructor [].' With `..` out of the expression grammar the leftover token is the S0201 an unexpected token gets, which is what jsonata 2.2.2 reports here too.

A predicate is the filter operator '[ ... ]' (docs.jsonata.org/path-operators), not the array constructor the range operator is confined to, so a bare range is not legal there; the doubled form a[[1..3]] is. jsntrs answered [2,3,4] before jsntrs-uql; jsonata 2.2.2 rejects it as well.

UNRESOLVED, and pinned only to catch an accidental change. This is a CONSEQUENCE of removing `..` from the expression grammar, not something the documentation decides: docs.jsonata.org/numeric-operators says only 'The sequence generator can only be used within an array constructor []', and `[(1..3)]` IS within an array constructor — the further rule that the range must be an ELEMENT of the constructor rather than nested inside a block within it appears nowhere in the documentation. jsntrs answered [1,2,3] before jsntrs-uql and answers S0202 now; jsonata 2.2.2 also answers S0202, but agreement with the reference is not authority. See jsntrs-2rp.

jsntrs answered [2] before jsntrs-uql: `..` bound looser than `?`, so the range was read as the conditional's else branch. Recognising `..` only between two elements of the constructor makes the whole conditional the range's LHS, which is jsonata 2.2.2's reading too.
